en: *Pabāna-kye-si-pa-tang* (in the Tang language: *Bu-zhi-jingang-niansong-yi*).
Homage to Vajrapāṇi! He who is the support of all Buddhas, who possesses the manifold practices of Samantabhadra, and who abides in this originally existent body.
Beginningless and endless quiescence, Exercising wondrous power to grant all vows;
The King who accords with the three poisons, Transforming the kalpas and making them supple and harmonious,
He rescues all sentient beings, Leading them from the state of ordinary beings into the stage of Buddhahood.
All shall be accomplished in this present life. Now, following the exposition of the meaning of recitation:
if there are bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, or upāsikās who delight in practicing the heart-mantra of the King of the Vidyārāja Krodha (Kumārarāja), [they should proceed as follows].
One should establish the maṇḍala by purifying the site according to the Dharma.
To practice the preliminary gate, one should sit facing east,
having prepared the necessary offerings of food, drink, incense, and flowers.
According to one's capacity, one should arrange matters so that everything is kept clean.
Having entered the maṇḍala, one should pay universal homage to all Buddhas with a single mind,
taking refuge and aspiring to attain perfect enlightenment.
Then, sit in the full lotus posture (*paryaṅka*) or the half-lotus posture (*ardhaparyaṅka*).
Anoint your hands with fragrant clay to prepare for the various mudrās.
Next, clarify the three families and perform the protection of the body.
The various ritual manuals are known to me, so they are not transcribed here in detail.
Next, one should sit upright with the body straightened and still all discursive thoughts.
One should contemplate that one's own body arises entirely from causes in previous lives.
These form the four great elements and five aggregates.
When one seeks their reality in each instance, nothing is found; they are impermanent and subject to decay.
Arising swiftly and ceasing swiftly, they are identical with form and identical with emptiness.
Having thus attained clear and definitive faith and understanding,
that which is capable of observation cannot be extinguished;
it becomes true wisdom.
It pervades the entire Dharma-realm,
its measure equal to empty space;
out of great compassion, it arises from the Truth to manifest its function.
Then, one should visualize one’s own body as being identical in majesty and demeanor to that of the Honored One—neither one nor different.
Furthermore, one should bind the previously mentioned Samādhi-Vajra-mudrā;
placing it upon the heart, one recites the Heart Mantra, saying:
Oṃ hrīḥ jvaḥ. Through the empowerment of this mudrā and mantra, the practitioner’s mind becomes one with the deity;
while raising the mudrā to the head, they recite the mantra.
Oṃ [bhu]ḥ. By means of this mudrā and the empowerment of this mantra, one becomes identical to the deity.
One should likewise apply the mudrā to the forehead, the right shoulder, the left shoulder, and the heart and throat.
All should recite the Armor Mantra:
Oṃ vīra. By virtue of this mudrā and the empowerment of this mantra, one immediately becomes armored in the vajra-mail, incapable of being harmed by any.
Through the power of the aforementioned contemplative practices and the empowerment of reciting mantras,
the practitioner’s body becomes indistinguishable from that of the deity;
the Buddhas bestow upon them predictions of enlightenment, and the nāgas and devas turn to them in reverent devotion.
One will certainly attain unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
Regarding the mudrā of the vajra-kīla: insert the right ring finger between the left ring finger and the little finger.
Insert the right middle finger between the left middle finger and index finger;
the left hand is likewise.
The remaining fingers have their tips touching one another.
Visualize it as the form of a flaming vajra;
place the thumbs on the ground,
strike down, and pull upward.
Recite this once, up to three times, and then stop.
Visualize the boundary according to its intended size;
it will immediately become a vajra-solid boundary.
The mantra is:
Oṃ kili kili vajra vajri-bhūra bandha bandha hūṃ phaṭ. By means of this mudrā and the empowerment of this mantra, [the binding is accomplished].
Extending downward to the vajra-limit, it is entirely like a vajra-throne;
neither celestial Māras nor any obstructors can cause harm or affliction.
Next is the vajra-wall boundary of the cardinal and intermediate directions.
The mudrā of the boundary corresponds to the previous earth-boundary;
extend the two thumbs and hold them upright,
with their sides touching like the shape of a wall.
Circumambulate the body three times to the right.
By fixing the mind upon its dimensions, it immediately becomes a vajra fortress, solid and unassailable;
even the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas cannot transgress it.
How much more so for all other beings who are difficult to subdue;
none can approach them.
The mantra is as follows:
Oṃ (1) śara śara (2) vajraprakāra (3) hūṃ phaṭ. Next, the practitioner should visualize an eight-petaled lotus flower within the maṇḍala.
Above was a lion throne;
upon the throne was a pavilion made of the seven treasures,
from which hung various necklaces, silken banners, and canopies.
Rows of precious pillars hung with exquisite celestial garments;
clouds of incense were spread everywhere,
raining down various flowers while the sounds of all manner of music resounded.
Having performed this visualization— of precious vases, *argha* offerings, celestial exquisite food and drink,
and lamps made of *maṇi* gems—
one should bind the mudrā of the Great Gaganagañja.
Form the mudrā by joining the palms at the heart;
curve the two index fingers into the shape of a jewel,
and extend both thumbs to press against the bases of the index fingers.
Interlace the middle fingers of both hands, with the right over the left on the outside;
when the hands are thus joined, the mudrā is perfected.
Recite the mantra as follows:
Oṃ gagana-svabhāva-vajra hūṃ. By means of binding this mudrā and reciting this mantra for empowerment, all imagined objects of offering and so forth [are purified].
The true and undifferentiated noble assembly enjoys it.
For the Jewel Chariot mudrā: interlace both hands with the palms facing upward;
cross the index fingers so that they touch each other horizontally.
Place both thumbs beneath the roots of the index fingers and visualize them as a chariot of the seven precious jewels;
the Vajra-ha shall mount it and travel through the air.
Upon reaching the palace of the tutelary deity,
recite the mantra three times.
The mantra is as follows:
Oṃ dūru dūru hūṃ. By means of empowering this mudrā and mantra, the seven-jeweled chariot proceeds to the supreme palace.
Visualize that the Great Sage, the Principal Deity, together with all his retinue, ascends the chariot.
Requesting the chariot and carriage, in accordance with the previous seal:
with the thumbs of both hands facing toward oneself, flick the middle fingers;
recite the mantra three times.
The mantra is as follows:

Namaḥ siddhye dhyānikānāṃ sarvatathāgatānām (2) oṃ (2) vāgīśvarī-janakarṣaṇye he he jaya svāhā (6) bhagavati (7) svāhā (7). By forming this mudrā and reciting the mantra with empowerment, [the deity] is summoned and sent forth.
The assembly of noble ones comes from their original palaces and,
arriving at the site of practice, dwells therein supported by space.
The Samaya of the Honored One descends as the seal of the site of practice.
For the seal of the sign: interlace the two hands with the palms facing inward to form fists;
insert the right thumb into the left palm and beckon the left thumb toward oneself.
The mantra is:
Oṃ vajra-dṛk he he jaha jahā hūṃ phaṭ svāhā. By means of the empowerment of this mantra-seal (mudrā), [the rite is accomplished].
The Honored Deity, not failing its original vow,
gathered at the site of practice (*maṇḍala*).
Stepping forward and casting down the seals (*mudrā*), each seal was positioned correctly one after another.
Lift the right foot toward the left, cutting through the void;
rotate to the right each day until it strikes the ground.
Then shift the left foot to the right, standing as before.
He then lifted his left foot toward the right, cutting through the empty air;
he then brought it down to the ground on the left, bending his knee.
He then raised his left hand with the index finger extended and the rest of the fingers clenched into a fist.
Press the side of the index finger with the thumb.
Visualize grasping a three-pronged vajra and extend the arms with great force toward the left in a threatening posture.
Insert the right hand’s thumb into the palm.
Grasp it with the middle and index fingers;
extend both the index and little fingers.
With maximum effort, let the arms hang down with the backs of the hands facing outward.
The figure of Mṛtyu appears with eyes wide in anger, gazing to the left;
his remaining arms all hold implements as does the Principal Deity,
and he is likewise accompanied by bodhisattvas and others.
Whenever one thinks of wiping the vessel with the hand, one should recite the Vessel-Wiping Mantra, saying: *Oṃ kṣa*.
One should further imagine that the threefold majestic flames of the entire body blaze forth like the conflagration at the end of an eon.
It penetrates to all worlds throughout the ten directions,
extensively performing the Buddha-work by illuminating, touching, and awakening through speech.
May all Tathāgatas who have newly attained the Way swiftly turn the wheel of Dharma.
Those who deliver sentient beings shatter their small vessels;
those who face nirvana are exhorted to remain for a long time.
Next, one should exhort the assembly of bodhisattvas to make vows.
May all of you swiftly realize unsurpassed bodhi;
in the interim, be careful not to fall back or become disheartened.
Furthermore, you should inspire those of the two vehicles.
He removes the fetters of the childish and causes them to be endowed with the profound wisdom of emptiness of the Mahāyāna;
wherever the majestic light reaches the realm of ordinary beings,
it eliminates the seeds of defilement within the storehouse consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*).
Forever free from the three miserable realms, they shall fulfill the practices of Samantabhadra;
as for those in the animal and hungry ghost realms, they shall never again undergo such births after this present life.
One should likewise contemplate all the various hells.
It utterly destroys and leaves no remainder of sinful beings;
it liberates all evil Māras who have resolved upon Bodhicitta;
and those encountered by it are subdued, expelled, and driven to retreat.
When such a duration of benefit has been completed,
visualize that the majestic flames are withdrawn and gathered within the body;
thereafter, emerge from meditative absorption.
Next, once again, sit according to the original procedure.
For the upper Vajra-net mudrā, follow the previous wall mudrā; join the two thumbs and press them against the lower joints of the index fingers.
Recite the mantra three times.
Rotate it three or two times clockwise on the head.
The mantra is as follows:
Oṃ viśpro naḥ kṣa-vajra-bhañjara hūṃ phaṭ. By means of this empowerment through the mantra of the Net Mudrā (Jāla-mudrā).
It shall become a vajra-firm net.
This is the *guhyasīvanavartamudrā* (the secret-sewing-whirling seal).
As for the form of the seal: with the left hand covering the back of the right hand, extend both thumbs.
Recite the mantra three times and circumambulate the body three times to the right,
visualizing outside the vajra wall.
Surrounded by flames.
The mantra is:
Oṃ āsaṃgini hūṃ phaṭ. Next, holding the arghya vessel near the forehead, visualize bathing the feet of the noble assembly.
For the mudrā of universal offering (*samantapūjā*), join both hands in *añjali* with the right hand placed over the left;
the gesture is completed by interlacing the fingers at their first joints.
Recite the mantra three times.

Contemplate with focused attention the immeasurable and boundless ocean-clouds of ointment incense, ocean-clouds of powdered incense, ocean-clouds of burning incense, ocean-clouds of flower garlands, ocean-clouds of radiant lamps, ocean-clouds of food and drink, and ocean-clouds of clothing.
The mantra for making all objects of offering and so forth pure, and for performing extensive and universal offerings, is as follows:
*Namaḥ sarvatathāgatebhyo viśvamukhebhyaḥ svāhā oṃ ānaya ānaya sphara hīṃ gaganaketa svāhā*. The heart-mantra of the deity is as follows:
Oṃ kheḥ kheḥ khaṃ khuḥ khūḥ. Next, one should further contemplate that one’s own body is no different from that of the deity.
Holding a rosary of *vajra* seeds,
recite the previously mentioned heart-mantra (*hṛdaya-mantra*).
While reciting with right mindfulness, visualize the form of the deity.
Either one contemplates all the syllables of the mantra,
or one contemplates the mantra-syllables upon the heart of the deity,
or one performs the recitation with a mind corresponding to tranquility.
Neither too hurried nor too slow, and not too small [in scale],
once the prescribed limit is completed and the mind wishes to rest,
one must nevertheless remain for a long duration in the visualization of the deity.
Again, offer argha water while forming the mudrā of universal offering; perform the mental offering and recite the root mantra.
Next, form the mudrā of the secret seam of the fire-enclosure (*agniparikṣepa*);
it is completed by turning once counter-clockwise above the head.
Next, having dissolved the boundary, perform the mudrā for descending to the ritual site and sweep it outward.
Visualize that the assembly of holy ones returns to their palaces.
Next, perform the mudrā for protecting the body.
Perform the previous mudrā at the five places, reciting the respective root mantras for each.

Next, recite the Mahācakra-vajra mantra twenty-one times. [This portion is omitted here as it is transcribed according to other versions; it is said that one may employ either method. By virtue of reciting this mantra, [the desired result is attained].
All transgressions of the rules of conduct shall be extinguished without remainder; their merit will not be in vain.
As for the three methods—pacification, enrichment, and subjugation:
The details are as extensively set forth in the Susiddhikara Sūtra.
One should know that for the rite of painting an image for the purpose of accomplishing any siddhi, the merit is vast;
the image should be made according to the prescribed measurements of one cubit (hasta), and it must be purified according to the ritual procedures.
In the illustration, the principal deity is entirely blue in color;
he gazes to the right with his right leg extended and his left knee bent,
while his upper right hand hangs downward.
Bend the thumb into the palm;
grasp it with the middle finger;
extend the remaining two fingers with the back of the hand facing outward.
Next, hold the peach with the hand and let it hang down.
Next, extend the palm downward;
within the palm, there are flames.
Next, he holds an iron axe in his hand;
next, a jade ring; next, he extends his fingers in a threatening gesture, upon which there are wheels.
Next, clench the fist and press the thumb against the side of the index finger.
Next, form the noose.
Next, extend all five fingers.
The nails are long and sharp, with the palms facing upward;
the left hand holds a bow,
and the right hand, near the upper one, holds a three-pronged mallet.
Extend the arms upward.
Next, [hold] a sword.
Next, grasp a round stone.
Next is the short-handled mallet, shaped like a heavy wheel;
next, two arrows;
next, a staff.
Next, the single-pronged vajra:
next, extend the palms with the palms facing upward, and join the tips of the index fingers and thumbs.
Next, upon the jewel-staff, the portion near the handle is coarse and gradually tapers toward the tip.
With the palm extended downward,
the palm is adorned with a wreath of flames.
All are spread out and upright;
their colors likewise feature dragons as crowns, garlands, and necklaces,
as well as bracelets for the hands and feet, waist-bands, and so forth.
With furrowed brows and a fierce gaze, his sharp fangs bared;
wearing a square skirt and a parasol, both of crimson hue,
the Māra Pāpīyas prostrated himself upon the ground.
He has four arms and his entire body is blue in color.
His faces are turned upward as he seeks mercy and begs for life.
He extends his right hand with its five fingers raised near his forehead in the gesture of taking refuge (*namaskāra-mudrā*).
With his left hand he grasps something from the ground;
in his two hands there is a dragon,
which he binds behind his elbow.
His hair was red and disheveled,
appearing as if he were in a state of great terror;
his head was near the right foot of the Great Sage.
To the left and right of the principal deity (iṣṭadevatā) are two Vajrakumāras,
both entirely red in color with radiant and robust physiques.
As for the one on the right side:
The right hand holds a peach;
the left hand grasps a sword, poised downward as if to strike the King of Māra.
Her hair hangs down behind her and is of a crimson color.
The figure on the left side is drawing a bow to the left, aiming at the head of the Māra;
his topknot is the color of red silk.
The character for "right" here, however, refers to the left.
The left character is actually on the right;
this is for concealment.
*The Ritual Manual for the Practice of the Step-Throwing Vajra*, one fascicle.
